title: Attachment, the clutching thief

segments.voice: Yesterday, pride, ahankar, the thief that slips in last and answers to your own name. Your line was the last thief.

A small girl at the beach scoops up a fistful of wet sand. She loves it, so she squeezes, and the tighter she squeezes, the faster it runs out between her fingers. Her father, beside her, holds his sand in an open palm, and it just stays there, catching the light. Same sand, same love, different hands. The Gurus have a word for the closed fist: moh, attachment, and the Guru Granth Sahib names it among the thieves that live inside the body. This thief is slippery in its own way, because it looks so much like love.
screen: `A FISTFUL OF SAND.` → `THE OPEN PALM.` → `MOH: THE CLOSED FIST.`

segments.voice: First, the list. In a hymn by Guru Amar Das, in paraphrase: within this body live five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride; they plunder the nectar, and the self-willed don't even notice. Second, what moh is not. Sikhs live as householders, with families, jobs and kitchens, so moh can't mean loving your family, and the Gurus don't ask anyone to walk out on home to beat it. Guru Nanak names its reach in Rag Asa, in paraphrase: attachment to family, attachment to all our work; give up attachment, it is all corruption. Not the family. Not the work. The attachment: love that has turned into grip. This person must stay exactly as they are, this house, this job, this version of my life, or I can't breathe. Third, the open hand. In the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with yogis who had left the world behind, he gives them a picture of living inside it: as the lotus stays untouched in the water, as the duck swims through the stream, so the one who keeps the Word in mind crosses the world-ocean. The lotus is in the water. It just doesn't drown. Fourth, why it counts as a thief. Clutching steals the very thing it's guarding. The grip makes a friend feel watched, a grown child feel smothered, a good evening feel too small to enjoy because it might end. The love was real. The fist is what spoils it.
screen: `FIVE THIEVES IN THE BODY.` · `NOT THE FAMILY. THE GRIP.` · `THE LOTUS IN THE WATER.` · `CLUTCHING STEALS WHAT IT GUARDS.` · then, large: `HOLD, DON'T CLUTCH.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and bring to mind someone or something you love and are afraid to lose; let the fear be there. Then, breath by breath, picture that love resting in your open palm, the way the sand rested in the father's hand: not thrown away, not squeezed, held. If your fingers start to curl, let them open again, and if you pray, hold that person before God with open hands.
Attachment. Moh: love that clutches, named among the thieves in the Gurus' list. Not the love itself; the grip. Today's word.
Your line: hold, don't clutch. Like the lotus: in the water, and not drowning. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of moh as one of the five thieves (panj chor) and seek to overcome it while living fully as householders, through remembrance of the Name and the Guru's teaching rather than by leaving family life.

original.note: Gurmukhi: attachment, the clinging kind of love; in the Granth it often appears as ਮੋਹੁ.

trapdoor: what you thought: attachment means loving people too much.
what it means: moh is love that grips, trying to keep a person or a life from changing.
what a scholar hears: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar: Guru Amar Das names moh among the thieves living in the body.

chat.says: If attachment is a thief, does that mean Sikhs should love their families less?
options: No. Sikhs live as householders. It's the grip that's the thief, not the love itself.
Yes. To beat attachment, you step back from family and live more on your own.
No. Attachment means loving things like money; loving people is never a problem.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak asks you to drop the attachment, not the family. Moh is love turned into grip; the lotus lives in the water without drowning.

moh.meaning: attachment: love that has turned into a clutching grip

notes: Editor pass: softened the claim that the Gurus all married and raised families (now 'Sikhs live as householders'), removed 'never', and stopped calling moh harder to catch than pride, since day 1401 called pride the hardest.
Please confirm Ang 600 for 'is dehi andar panch chor vaseh, kaam krodh lobh moh ahankaara' and the paraphrase (plunder the nectar; the self-willed don't notice).
Please confirm Ang 356 for Guru Nanak's 'moh kutamb moh sabh kaar, moh tum tajahu sagal vekaar' and that reading it as 'drop the attachment, not the family' is fair.
